input: In this example, the steady heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall is calculated. The wall, which has a thickness of 150 mm, separates two process streams from one another. The purpose of the example is to illustrate how the basic conduction relationship can be applied to a simple plane wall once the relevant properties and dimensions have been specified, and to show the order of magnitude of the heat flux that results under the stated conditions. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 175 K. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux can be obtained by multiplying the thermal conductivity by the temperature difference and dividing by the wall thickness. Expressing the thickness in metres gives a value of 0.15 m. Substituting the values into this relationship gives a heat flux of 18667 W m-2. This result illustrates the combined influence of the material property and the geometry: a relatively thin wall of a material with a moderate thermal conductivity can nevertheless transmit a substantial heat flux when it is subjected to a large temperature difference, and the calculation provides a convenient reference point against which more complete estimates, incorporating additional thermal resistances, can subsequently be compared. It should be noted that this estimate is based on conduction through the wall alone: the surface (film) resistances have been excluded from the estimate, and including them would result in a lower flux, since each film would add a further resistance in series with the wall itself. In a more complete treatment, those resistances would be added to the resistance of the wall itself, and the overall temperature difference would be shared between the films and the metal in proportion to their respective resistances, reducing the temperature difference that is actually available across the wall.
target: Calculate the steady heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall. The wall is 150 mm thick and separates two process streams. Its thermal conductivity is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 175 K. The wall is treated as a slab: its faces are large beside its thickness, so the flow of heat is one-dimensional, normal to the faces, and steady. Steady means the temperature at each point of the wall no longer changes with time: the heat entering one face leaves by the other, and none accumulates in the metal. One-dimensional means the temperature varies only through the thickness, not along the faces. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is calculated as the conductivity multiplied by the temperature difference and divided by the thickness. The thickness in metres is 0.15 m. Substitution gives a heat flux of 18667 W m-2. The size of the flux follows from the thickness and the conductivity together: at the same thickness and the same temperature difference, a poorer conductor passes a smaller flux in proportion to its conductivity, because the relation is linear in each of its terms. The estimate is a conduction-only figure. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, because each film adds a resistance in series with the wall, and the temperature difference left to drive conduction through the metal falls by the drop across the films. The films are the fluid layers at the two faces, and their resistance depends on the fluids and their motion, not on the wall; that dependence is why the estimate keeps them separate. The stated flux is therefore the value for the wall alone, at the temperature difference measured across the metal itself.
